analysis.one_liner: Keeps medical bills off credit reports for a year and erases paid-off medical debt within 45 days.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 70 cosponsors — 69 Democrats and 1 Republican — but never got a committee markup or a floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred debt collectors and credit bureaus from putting medical bills on a person's credit report until a full year after the bill went to collection. It also would have required paid-off and settled medical debts to come off credit reports within 45 days, and forced collectors to send advance notice — with the exact reporting date and information about insurance coverage and financial assistance — before ever reporting a medical debt. The point was to give people time to resolve billing disputes, insurance claims, or charity care before a hospital bill wrecked their credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with medical debt. Instead of a hospital bill hitting their credit report within weeks, they would get a year to contest the bill, work it through their insurer, or apply for financial assistance — and if they paid or settled it during that window, it would never appear at all. Fully paid or settled medical debts already on reports would come off within 45 days. Because medical debt on a credit report can mean higher loan rates, denied applications, and trouble renting a home, this would have shielded millions of households from credit damage caused by bills that often stem from insurance disputes and billing errors.

how_it_helps.text: Blocks medical debt from appearing on a credit report until one year after it is placed for collection, giving consumers time to resolve it first.
Requires fully paid or settled medical debts to be removed from credit reports within 45 days of payment or settlement.

Forces collectors to send advance notice before reporting a medical debt, stating the exact date reporting could begin and telling the consumer they can pursue insurance coverage or financial assistance in the meantime.
If the debt is paid or settled during the one-year window — by the consumer or by an insurance company — it can never be reported to a credit bureau.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection agencies lose their most powerful lever — the threat of credit damage — for at least a year on every medical debt, and must delete paid and settled medical debts. The three national credit bureaus lose a large category of data they currently compile and sell. Lenders would see less information about unpaid medical obligations when screening borrowers, and the bill's backers argue the trade is better information quality; critics would say lenders and other borrowers bear some of that cost through slightly tighter credit or higher rates.

drawbacks.text: The debt itself does not disappear and collection calls are not restricted — the bill delays and limits credit reporting only, so people would still owe the money and still hear from collectors.

Lenders would lose visibility into unpaid medical obligations for up to a year, which in a good-faith objection means some borrowers who should be priced as riskier would not be, potentially tightening credit or raising rates for others.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief to consumers is concrete and the cost is modest. Medical bills frequently arise from insurance disputes, denied claims, and billing errors, and a one-year reporting delay directly addresses that gap rather than erasing legitimate debt — collectors can still pursue payment, and after a year unpaid debts can still be reported. The real trade-off is that lenders lose some risk information, a diffuse cost spread across the credit market rather than a concentrated benefit. On balance the bill targeted a specific, well-defined harm with a narrow tool.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on April 7, 2020, with 63 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
It eventually gathered 70 cosponsors — 69 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans — but the committee took no further action on it.
The bill's action history ends with the committee referral: no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection agencies and the credit bureaus are better off, since the restrictions never took effect; medical debt continued to appear on credit reports largely as before.

for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only Republican support.

against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the bill never received a markup or floor vote during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was measured only in sponsorship: 69 of 231 House Democrats signed on alongside just 1 of 197 House Republicans, and no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill strips their main leverage on medical debts: no credit reporting for a year, mandatory advance notice, and deletion of paid or settled medical debts. Collectors could still call and pursue payment, but the credit-report threat that converts unpaid bills into payment would be blunted.

The three national bureaus would lose a large category of data — medical collections — that they currently compile into reports, plus the report volume and disputes tied to it. Medical debt is a frequent source of credit report errors, so the bill also cuts into the correction business built around it.

Lenders would get less information about unpaid medical obligations for up to a year, which the bill's own title frames as a loss of 'perfect information' — though removing bills that often reflect insurance disputes rather than borrower behavior could also mean better-quality signals on the debts that remain.

Providers can still bill and collect — the bill explicitly leaves collection activity alone — but the required notice steers patients toward insurance claims and financial assistance during the reporting freeze, which could shift some balances to charity care or insurer payment.
